extracted.intended_audience: educational institutions, Title IX administrators, administrative-law practitioners, and stakeholders/commenters on federal rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: Preamble to the Department of Education's final Title IX regulations responding to public comments, explaining legal and procedural standards (APA, Executive Orders, case law), and describing requirements for recipients' grievance processes and agency rulemaking practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-agency coordination / avoid inconsistencies
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulations should be coordinated across agencies to avoid being "inconsistent, incompatible, or duplicative" with other agencies' regulations; interagency review (via OMB and other agencies) is part of that coordination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department shared the proposed regulations with OMB before publication of the NPRM so OMB could provide other Federal agencies (including SBA Advocacy and agencies that enforce Title IX) an opportunity to review and comment. This interagency review process is designed to avoid inconsistent or duplicative regulations and to promote coordination. The Department cannot control other agencies but must take reasonable steps to effectuate coordination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure of basis for agency action
rubrics_metrics.description: To permit meaningful judicial and public review, an agency must disclose the basis of its action; rulemaking and its preamble (and responses to comments) serve to disclose that basis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department states it is disclosing its reasons through the NPRM, the preamble to the final rule, and its responses to the over 124,000 public comments received; transparency in the rulemaking record is required for meaningful review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasoned explanation when changing policy/position
rubrics_metrics.description: When an agency departs from past practice or changes position, it must display awareness of the change and provide good reasons for it; a reasoned explanation is required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The agency need not show the new reasons are better than the old, only that the new policy is permissible under the statute, that there are good reasons for it, and that the agency believes it to be better. The preamble must explain the rationale for changes (e.g., adoption/adaption of Supreme Court framework, changes to §106.45).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of reliance interests
rubrics_metrics.description: When changing longstanding policies, the agency must be cognizant of and account for reliance interests engendered by the prior policy and explain any decision that disregards those facts or circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reliance interests may be substantial for students and institutions who relied on prior guidance to vindicate rights or set procedures; the agency's explanation for change should address these reliance interests where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaningful opportunity to comment (APA and Executive Orders)
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies must give interested persons a meaningful opportunity to participate in rulemaking; Executive Order 12866 generally recommends comment periods of not less than 60 days, and case law typically views less than 30 days as inadequate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department published a 60-day comment period in the Federal Register and provided extensions (including additional days to account for e-rulemaking portal technical issues) and publicized those extensions on its website and in the Federal Register; the number of comments (over 124,000) is cited as evidence of meaningful participation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of appropriate data and provide a rational connection between facts and decision
rubrics_metrics.description: An agency must examine relevant data, acknowledge data limitations, use the most appropriate available data, and draw a rational connection between the underlying facts and its regulatory decisions (including economic cost/benefit analysis).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters criticized reliance on datasets (e.g., CRDC, Clery Act) with known limitations; the Department defends using the best available data and provides a Regulatory Impact Analysis discussing costs and benefits. Failure to examine relevant data or to make a rational connection may render a rule arbitrary and capricious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Initial Regulatory Flexibility Analysis (IRFA) requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The NPRM included an initial regulatory flexibility analysis (IRFA) as required where rulemaking may have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The IRFA was part of the NPRM record and commenters' critiques of economic analysis were addressed in the preamble and RIA sections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responding to and considering public comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies must review, consider, and respond to public comments on proposed regulations and, where appropriate, make changes to the proposed rule in light of those comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department states it reviewed over 124,000 comments and made changes reflected in the final regulations; the preamble documents how commenters' views informed specific revisions and explains which stakeholder inputs were considered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grievance process fairness and due process protections (§106.45)
rubrics_metrics.description: When a complainant files a formal complaint alleging sexual harassment, a recipient's investigation must be fair and impartial, applying strong procedural protections for both parties to produce reliable factual outcomes consistent with constitutional protections and fundamental fairness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The final regulations aim to provide clear options and honor complainants' wishes about how a recipient should respond; they require supportive measures for complainants (with or without a formal complaint), strong procedural protections during investigations, and safeguards to protect both parties' rights. §106.44(b)(2) clarifies that the Assistant Secretary will not deem a recipient's different responsibility determination as deliberate indifference solely because the Department would have weighed the evidence differently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alignment with Title IX text and Supreme Court framework
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department intends to better align Title IX implementing regulations with the text and purpose of Title IX and with Supreme Court precedent (adopting and adapting the Court's three-part framework for sexual harassment: definition of actionable sexual harassment, actual knowledge, and deliberate indifference).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The preamble explains rationale for adopting/adapting the Supreme Court's framework for administrative enforcement and discusses how changes to §106.30 (definitions) and §106.45 (grievance process) implement that alignment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect for First Amendment and academic freedom (regulate conduct, not speech)
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulations must respect constitutional rights; Title IX regulations address conduct in exchange for federal funds, not academic speech, and therefore do not impermissibly infringe recipients' First Amendment rights when they are narrowly tailored to a compelling governmental interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department explains that the final regulations do not dictate curricula or admissions and that restrictions on association/speech can be upheld where they serve compelling state interests and are narrowly tailored (citing Roberts, Boys Scouts v. Dale, Keyishian, Rumsfeld). The preamble argues the regulations appropriately qualify institutional rights to further Title IX's objectives without unlawfully burdening First Amendment freedoms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preservation of recipients' discretion over sanctions and non-Title IX conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: The regulations do not dictate the particular disciplinary sanctions a recipient may impose and do not preclude recipients from addressing conduct that falls outside Title IX through their own codes of conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: §106.45(b)(3)(i) was revised to clarify that dismissal of a formal Title IX complaint (or allegations therein) does not preclude action under another provision of the recipient's code of conduct; recipients retain discretion in disciplinary decisions even where they follow §106.45 procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of established legal review channels and approvals
rubrics_metrics.description: Publication and finalization of significant regulations involve review and approval by other legal offices (e.g., Assistant Attorney General for Civil Rights) and compliance with Executive Order review processes (e.g., EO 12250).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department notes the Assistant Attorney General for Civil Rights reviewed and approved the proposed regulations for publication in the Federal Register in accordance with Executive Order 12250, as part of ensuring legal sufficiency and interagency coordination.
